reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its main communicative action is a screen-recorded tutorial demonstrating how to register for BitClub Network through an inviter's link and confirm the sponsor name. Although the website promotes earning Bitcoin through mining and uses testimonials, the supplied content does not show a payment requirement, guaranteed return, credential theft request, or tiered recruitment-earnings structure that would establish a scam mechanism.

opening.argument: The page does more than explain an account process: it places a Bitcoin-earning promise directly beside a registration funnel. The headline presents BitClub as an innovative and lucrative way to earn Bitcoin, while the adjacent panel asks whether the viewer is ready to earn Bitcoin and provides fields and a registration button. The narration then instructs viewers to follow an inviter's link and click sign-up. That is a concrete promise-action relationship: register through the supplied pathway in connection with the advertised earning opportunity, rather than merely learn about cryptocurrency.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a tutorial does not neutralize the solicitation visible in the tutorial. The reference opening acknowledges that the site promotes earning Bitcoin, but treats the absence of a proven payment requirement as decisive. That sets the bar too high for this category: the relevant conduct is the advertised earning opportunity linked to registration, and the page visibly combines both. The narration's step-by-step instructions make the pathway actionable, not merely informational.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The earning language does not show that registration provides a reward, much less that it is free or guaranteed. The video demonstrates only how to open an account through an inviter's link and click sign-up. The page's promotional wording and form establish an invitation to register, but they do not establish what happens afterward, whether any money is paid, or whether participation requires payment.

opening.argument: Several risk signals reinforce one another on the same screen: a prominent claim about earning money by mining Bitcoin, a mining-pool identity, a rotating member-testimonial section, and a form requesting personal contact information before registration. The page also frames the opportunity as lucrative and displays positive member experiences while the viewer is being directed toward the registration button. That combination is materially more persuasive than a neutral technical demonstration: it uses mining-income claims and social proof to encourage participation, while the supplied evidence gives no operational detail about the mining activity or how returns would be generated.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side isolates each missing element, but the concern arises from their combination. A screen recording can still function as promotional onboarding when it showcases income language, testimonials, and a live registration form. The absence of an explicit deposit instruction does not explain why the page pairs mining-income messaging with personal-data fields and a prominent registration call to action.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals show promotion, not a paid-mining return mechanism. The frames do not establish that a viewer purchases hashpower, joins a paid package, supplies funds, or receives recurring mining income. Testimonials and a registration form may make the page persuasive, but they do not prove the specific paid-mining pathway required for this subtype.

opening.argument: Although the narration calls the video a tutorial, its practical effect is promotional onboarding. Viewers are told to use an inviter-provided link, verify that the inviter's name appears, and complete registration. The destination page presents BitClub as a lucrative way to earn Bitcoin and places that message alongside the sign-up interface. The instructional format therefore serves as the delivery mechanism for directing viewers into the advertised opportunity: it reduces friction, confirms the sponsor relationship, and ends with the registration action rather than an evaluation of the service.
